summary:
The Unforgotten is an interactive, story-driven web experience that brings NASA’s missions on the Moon, Mars, and in Deep Space to life for kids and space enthusiasts. 
Addressing the "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars" challenge, our app transforms scattered technical archives into an engaging journey guided by Orion, an animated astronaut character. Users explore illustrated comic-style panels and watch NASA's real mission footage and photos. It helps enthusiasts explore missions without getting overwhelmed by scattered links by bringing mission data, historical photos, videos, and achievements together in one place. 
By pairing authentic NASA imagery and chronological timelines with a dedicated Pioneers section highlighting the people behind the missions, The Unforgotten preserves overlooked space history and makes STEM accessible, inspiring, and easy to understand for young learners.
details:
Backup Source Code & Assets: https://drive.google.com/file/d/10XlgQKhdZAMKx4kZgwOreaSL1Es10yvW/view?usp=drive_link

The Unforgotten is an interactive web platform built for the "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars" challenge. Instead of leaving young learners and space enthusiasts to sift through scattered technical databases, the app brings verified NASA mission archives, photos, and videos together into one guided experience led by Orion, an animated astronaut character.

Three Exploration Modules: Users journey across the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space through illustrated comic-style panels, visiting historic landing sites.

Interactive Mission Cards: Each rover, lander, and deep-space probe features a dedicated profile answering five core questions: Why was it launched? What did it achieve? How did it help humanity? Where is it right now? And when did it last send data?

Authentic NASA Media & Obstacle Stories: Real NASA mission footage and historical photographs are embedded directly alongside illustrated stories highlighting the engineering hardships each spacecraft overcame.

Chronological Timeline & Pioneers Section: A date-ordered timeline maps how missions unfolded across space history, while the Pioneers section spotlights the real scientists, engineers, and astronauts behind the hardware.

Transparent Sources Tab: Every NASA dataset, image, and video reference is organized in a dedicated Sources tab so users can explore the original archives directly.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Human missions often capture the public spotlight, while the robotic pioneers left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space quietly fade from memory. The Unforgotten preserves this overlooked space history and bridges the STEM accessibility gap. By translating dense telemetry and scattered archives into clear, visual stories, the platform helps kids, students, and space enthusiasts engage with real NASA science without feeling overwhelmed—while showing young learners that ordinary people from diverse backgrounds make extraordinary exploration possible.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

Frontend & Web Development: React, TypeScript, HTML5, CSS3, and Tailwind CSS built and deployed via Google AI Studio.

Visuals & Storytelling Assets: Google Nano Banana Pro (for custom comic-style panels and character illustrations of Orion), Gemini and Claude (for simplifying technical NASA mission logs into age-appropriate scripts), and official NASA image and video archives.

Creativity

Space history is usually told in dense, technical pages, and the people behind it are often left out. We rebuilt it so anyone can step in. We wrote and illustrated more than 100 comic panels across three stories (the Moon, Mars and deep space), led by an astronaut guide, Orion, in plain words.

Real NASA photos and video sit beside the panels, and mission cards give each machine its own page and status. We also put the people forward. Our Pioneers section introduces real engineers, scientists and astronauts from different backgrounds, each with one contribution to a mission, so students from any background can see themselves in space exploration.

The closing message is simple: the next entry on the timeline could be yours.

Factors considered

Audience. We wrote for school-age readers and casual space fans, using plain words, short sentences, and “New word” notes for anything technical.

Accessibility. The site uses a simple, consistent layout, readable text, and the same six questions for every mission.

Perspective. An astronaut guide, Orion, leads the stories, and our Pioneers section introduces real people from different backgrounds, so students can see themselves in space exploration.
